summary:
Across 17 evals (96 iterations total; 2 "negative" evals were intentionally skipped since they test that the agent should NOT trigger, and both variants correctly did not trigger in those cases), the two variants show a consistent but not absolute pattern: with_skill met the expected-output bar more often and passed more per-assertion checks in most evals, while without_skill was faster and cheaper to run in nearly every eval, sometimes dramatically so (e.g. several evals where without_skill's runtime/cost registered as ~0s/$0.00 vs with_skill's 15-36s and $0.13-$0.30, and in "corruption-not-quality-regression" and "qe-hardware-corruption-garbled" with_skill took noticeably longer, ~5 minutes vs ~4-5 minutes for without_skill, at comparable cost).

Expected-output pass rates: with_skill matched or exceeded without_skill in most evals (e.g. evaluation-coverage-assessment 1/3 vs 0/3, finish-reason-truncation-drift 3/3 vs 0/3, qe-regression-gate-missing 3/3 vs 1/3, qe-nondeterminism-vs-regression 3/3 vs 2/3), while both were tied at 100% in several others (output-contract-drift, qe-output-contract-drift's expected_output, qe-judge-model-validity, qe-baseline-missing, qe-eval-job-failed, qe-dataset-representativeness, qe-safety-refusal-rate, qe-token-truncation-vs-quality). In one eval (quality-regression-triage) both tied at 1/3, and without_skill's own assertion pass rate there was actually higher (12/12 vs 9/12) and it was favored on the single quality-pair comparison — a case where the aggregate expected-output match doesn't tell the full story. Confidence behind these expected-output judgments was mostly "high," though a few without_skill judgments were "medium" confidence, meaning those specific findings are somewhat less certain.

Per-assertion detail reveals important nuance an aggregate score would hide: many assertions passed for both variants (e.g. "always_passes" patterns on causes, enforcement mechanisms, A/B comparison checks), meaning those checks aren't differentiating the variants. Some assertions failed for both regardless of variant (e.g. "explains why running an eval job would not diagnose this," "requires a baseline... non-determinism" in qe-output-contract-drift, "EVAL check-id cited" in several evals) — these point to gaps in the underlying behavior or assertion design rather than a variant-specific weakness. A recurring "with_skill_passes_without_skill_fails" pattern appears specifically around citing check-IDs and explicitly noting that pipeline wiring/CI cannot be verified from AWS APIs alone (seen in finish-reason-truncation-drift and qe-regression-gate-missing), suggesting a specific behavioral difference concentrated in those checks rather than a uniform quality gap.

Where head-to-head quality comparisons were run, with_skill was favored somewhat more often in on balance (e.g. qe-baseline-missing 7 vs 1, qe-hardware-corruption-garbled 9 vs 2, qe-judge-model-validity 4 vs 1, qe-dataset-representativeness 5 vs 2, qe-token-truncation-vs-quality 5 vs 2, qe-safety-refusal-rate 4 vs 1), but several evals show ties or mixed/comparable results (output-contract-drift 5/3/3 comparable, qe-output-contract-drift 2/2/5 comparable, qe-eval-job-failed 2 vs 5 favoring without_skill, qe-regression-gate-missing 1 vs 1 tied). Confidence on these quality comparisons is generally "medium," so these differences should be read as directional tendencies rather than strong, certain findings. Many eval pairs (especially in evaluation-coverage-assessment and finish-reason-truncation-drift) had quality comparisons skipped entirely (0 of 3 pairs evaluated), so no quality verdict is available there.

Output consistency (run-to-run stability) varied by eval and didn't favor one variant uniformly: with_skill was "consistent" in several evals (finish-reason-truncation-drift, output-contract-drift, qe-output-contract-drift, qe-nondeterminism-vs-regression, qe-judge-model-validity, qe-baseline-missing, qe-dataset-representativeness, qe-safety-refusal-rate) while without_skill was rated "mostly_consistent" or "inconsistent" in some of the same evals; conversely without_skill was rated fully "consistent" in a few evals (qe-baseline-missing, qe-regression-gate-missing, qe-token-truncation-vs-quality) while with_skill was only "mostly_consistent" there. In evaluation-coverage-assessment both variants were rated "inconsistent," and in corruption-not-quality-regression and qe-hardware-corruption-garbled without_skill showed "inconsistent" results (with_skill's consistency data was partly null/missing in corruption-not-quality-regression, so no comparison is available there).

Overall, the pattern across this run set is a tradeoff: with_skill tends to meet expected-output criteria and pass assertions somewhat more often, and is judged moderately favorably in head-to-head quality comparisons, but runs longer and costs more in almost every eval, sometimes substantially (minutes vs seconds, or $0.82 vs $0.57 in the extreme case). Variant_b is consistently faster/cheaper and is occasionally more consistent run-to-run, but misses more expected-output and assertion checks, particularly around explicit check-ID citation and some explicit caveats about what can/cannot be verified from AWS APIs. Many individual assertions and a few whole-eval quality comparisons show no differentiation at all, and several specific behaviors (explaining why an eval job wouldn't diagnose a hardware/service issue, escalation recommendations) failed for both variants, indicating eval/assertion design gaps rather than a variant-specific issue.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in 1 of 3 runs (33%), while without_skill met it in 0 of 3 runs (0%). Both measurements carry high confidence, meaning the judgments behind these pass/fail calls are reasonably reliable even though the sample size is small (3 runs each).

Assertions: Across 18 assertion checks (6 distinct assertions x 3 runs), with_skill passed 6/18 (33%) and without_skill passed 0/18 (0%). Looking at the individual assertions, the same pattern repeats for every one of the 6 checks: each is marked "flaky" and with_skill passes it in 1 of 3 runs while without_skill fails it in all 3 runs. No assertion passed for both variants, and none passed for neither — without_skill failed uniformly across every assertion and every run, while with_skill showed partial, inconsistent success on every assertion. This is a notable and consistent pattern across the whole assertion set, not an isolated difference on one check.

Quality comparison: No side-by-side quality pairs could be evaluated (0 pairs evaluated, 3 skipped), so there is no direct quality judgment available to weigh against the pass-rate difference.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 1m38s and $0.82 per run; without_skill averaged 1m8s and $0.57 per run — without_skill ran roughly 30 seconds faster and cost about $0.25 less on average. Context window utilization was low for both (6.7% vs 4.6%), with no compaction events for either.

Output consistency: Neither variant was fully consistent across repeated runs. Variant_a was rated "inconsistent" on all 3 measured dimensions (consistency score 1.0), while without_skill was rated "inconsistent" on 2 dimensions and "consistent" on 1 (score 1.67), both with high-confidence judgments. So without_skill showed somewhat more run-to-run stability than with_skill, even though it did not pass the expected-output or assertion checks in any run.

Overall, the picture across dimensions is mixed rather than one-sided: with_skill met the expected output and individual assertions more often (though still only in a minority of runs), while without_skill was cheaper, faster, and marginally more consistent across runs. Given the small sample (3 runs per variant), the complete absence of quality-comparison data, and the fact that even with_skill's better pass rate is low (33%) and flaky, these results point to a task or set of assertions that neither variant reliably satisfies, rather than a clear difference in overall capability between the two variants.

output-contract-drift.summary:
Both variants were evaluated on the same chat task (3 runs each). The triggering behavior fired in all cases, and both variants met the overall "expected output" criterion in 3/3 runs with high confidence — this dimension shows no difference between them.

On detailed assertions, both variants had identical pass rates overall (15/21, 71%), and in fact matched exactly on every individual assertion:
- Three assertions always passed for both (quantifying parse-failure rate, recommending non-voluntary enforcement like schema validation, recommending a durable detection mechanism).
- One assertion ("requires a pre-change baseline") was flaky for both, passing 2/3 times (without_skill's passes were at only medium confidence, with_skill's at high).
- One assertion (about noting dependency on Bedrock invocation logging) was flaky for both, passing only 1/3 times.
- One assertion (citing an evaluation/telemetry check-id) failed for both variants in all runs — this suggests either the assertion is too strict or neither variant's behavior satisfies it; it's not a point of differentiation but a shared gap.

So assertion-level results show no differences between the variants — all variation is shared across both.

Where the variants diverge is in cost/runtime and in softer quality and consistency measures. without_skill ran much faster (~10s avg vs ~32s avg for with_skill) and cost less (~$0.09 vs ~$0.27), with slightly lower context utilization (4.4% vs 5.1%); one of with_skill's three runs exceeded the 30s runtime threshold. On pairwise LLM-judged quality (3 pairs evaluated, medium average confidence), with_skill was favored in 5 criterion-comparisons, without_skill in 3, with 3 rated comparable — a modest edge toward with_skill, concentrated mostly in "accuracy," while "actionability" leaned slightly toward without_skill and "completeness" was mixed. This is a small sample (3 pairs) so the signal is not strong.

Output consistency across repeated runs was rated "consistent" for with_skill (score 3.0) versus "mostly_consistent" for without_skill (score 2.0), both at high confidence — indicating with_skill's outputs varied slightly less run-to-run, though without_skill's outputs were still rated as mostly consistent rather than erratic.

Overall: the two variants are functionally equivalent on the explicit pass/fail criteria (expected output and assertions), with the only shared weakness being the uncited telemetry check-id assertion. The differences that do appear are tradeoffs rather than clear regressions — without_skill is markedly faster and cheaper, while with_skill shows slightly higher-rated quality (modest, low-sample-size signal) and slightly more run-to-run consistency.

corruption-not-quality-regression.summary:
This investigation eval ran 3 trials each. The trigger behavior itself fired reliably in all cases (3/3), so the underlying test scenario worked as intended.

Expected output: with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, medium confidence), while without_skill met it in 2 of 3 runs (67%, but with high confidence on that judgment). This is a modest gap, and the confidence pattern is mixed — with_skill's "pass" judgments are only medium-confidence, while without_skill's measurement (including its one miss) is high-confidence, so the shortfall for without_skill is reasonably well-established even though with_skill's perfect score rests on a weaker confidence basis.

Assertions (18 total checks, 6 unique assertions x 3 runs each): with_skill passed 8/18 (44%), without_skill passed 9/18 (50%) — a small, likely not meaningful difference. Looking at individual assertions is more informative than the aggregate:
- One assertion ("identifies service-side/infra fault rather than model regression") passed consistently for both variants (3/3 each) — this doesn't differentiate them.
- Two assertions ("explains why an eval job wouldn't diagnose this" and "recommends escalation to incident triage/support") failed for both variants in all runs (0/3 each) — neither variant exhibits this behavior at all, suggesting a gap in both outputs or that this behavior is simply hard to elicit.
- One assertion ("declines the user's framing, doesn't present prompt edits as fix") showed a real split: with_skill passed only 1/3 while without_skill passed 3/3, favoring without_skill with high confidence on without_skill's side.
- Two other assertions ("reasoning that separates abrupt onset/partial traffic/no change" and "offers a way to quantify affected traffic share") were flaky for both, with with_skill slightly ahead on the traffic-quantification one and the two tying on the reasoning one.

Quality comparison: only 2 of 3 pairs could be evaluated (1 skipped), a small sample. Overall it was close — with_skill favored in 4 sub-judgments, without_skill in 3, 1 comparable — with high confidence but drawn from a thin set of pairs, so this should be read as roughly even rather than a clear edge either way. Per-criterion breakdowns (impact analysis, root cause, key findings, supporting evidence) each show near-even or tied splits between the two variants.

Runtime and cost: with_skill averaged 4m59s/$2.49, without_skill averaged 5m10s/$2.58 — a small difference (~11s, ~$0.09) favoring with_skill slightly, not likely to be practically significant. Both had low, similar context-window utilization (~11-12%) and no compaction events. No runs exceeded the runtime threshold for either.

Output consistency: with_skill has no consistency data reported (null), so nothing can be said about its run-to-run stability. Variant_b was flagged as "inconsistent" across all 4 measured dimensions with high confidence, indicating without_skill's outputs varied meaningfully between repeated runs. Since there's no comparable consistency measurement for with_skill, this is a one-sided finding — it tells us something concrete about without_skill's stability but can't be directly compared to with_skill.

Overall, the two variants performed similarly on cost, runtime, and aggregate assertion/quality metrics, with small differences in each direction. The most notable distinguishing signals are: with_skill's stronger (though lower-confidence) expected-output pass rate, a clear split favoring without_skill on the "declines user's framing" assertion, and a one-sided consistency flag on without_skill indicating run-to-run variability that cannot be contrasted against with_skill since no equivalent measurement exists for it. qe-nondeterminism-vs-regression.summary:
This evaluation covers a single chat-based eval with 3 repeated runs. The behavior under test (trigger) fired reliably for both variants (3/3).

**Expected output:** with_skill met the expected output in all 3 runs (100%, high confidence), while without_skill met it in 2/3 runs (67%, medium confidence). The medium confidence on without_skill's measurement means this gap, while a real difference, rests on a somewhat less certain judgment than with_skill's.

**Assertions:** Across 15 assertion instances (5 distinct assertions x 3 runs), with_skill passed 12/15 (80%) and without_skill passed 10/15 (67%). Breaking this down by individual assertion is informative:
- Three assertions (explaining output variability is expected, naming sampling parameters, being candid about non-determinism) passed 3/3 for both variants — these do not differentiate the variants.
- One assertion ("redirects reproducibility to aggregate evaluation on a fixed dataset rather than string equality") passed 3/3 for with_skill but only 1/3 for without_skill (flaky) — this is the main driver of the assertion-rate gap and the expected-output gap.
- One assertion ("at least one finding carries an EVAL check-id") failed for both variants in all runs (0/3) — this indicates either a problem with that specific behavior/assertion in both variants, or a prompt/assertion-design issue, rather than a difference between variants.

**Quality comparison:** Only 2 of 3 pairs could be evaluated for quality (1 skipped), limiting confidence in this dimension. Of those, overall quality judgments favored with_skill 3 times, without_skill once, with 4 comparable judgments, at medium average confidence. Per-criterion, with_skill was favored more often on accuracy and completeness, while actionability was roughly split (1 favor each, 1 comparable). Given the small pair count and medium confidence, this should be read as a mild, not strongly certain, directional signal toward with_skill's output quality.

**Runtime and cost:** without_skill was notably faster (~9s avg vs ~19s avg for with_skill) and cheaper (~$0.08 vs ~$0.16). Neither variant exceeded the 30s runtime threshold in the 2 evaluated pairs. Context window utilization was similar and low for both (~4.5-4.7%), with no compaction events for either.

**Output consistency:** with_skill was rated fully "consistent" across all three repeated-run dimensions (score 3.0, high confidence), while without_skill was "mostly consistent" (score 2.67, high confidence), with one dimension rated only mostly consistent rather than fully consistent.

**Overall picture:** with_skill shows higher and more confidently-measured expected-output and assertion pass rates, a mild quality edge (based on limited pairs), and slightly more run-to-run consistency. without_skill is substantially faster and cheaper to run. One assertion passed for both variants in every run (not differentiating) and one failed for both in every run (a shared gap, not a variant-specific issue). The clearest variant-specific difference is the flaky assertion about redirecting reproducibility claims, where without_skill was notably less reliable. These results represent a cost/speed vs. reliability/quality tradeoff rather than a clear overall difference, and some findings (quality comparison, expected-output confidence for without_skill) rest on limited sample sizes or medium confidence.
